definition: An identity with permissions policies that can be assumed by users, applications, or AWS services. Provides temporary credentials — no long-term access keys.
gotcha: Roles assumed via role chaining have a hard cap of 1 hour, regardless of the role's max session duration setting (which can be up to 12 hours for direct AssumeRole).

definition: A container for an IAM role that allows EC2 instances to assume the role and obtain temporary credentials automatically via the instance metadata service.
gotcha: An instance profile can contain only one role. The console creates one automatically when you attach a role to an EC2 instance, but the CLI/API requires creating it separately.

definition: Centralized access management (formerly AWS SSO) for multiple AWS accounts and business applications. Uses a single sign-on portal.
gotcha: This is the AWS-recommended way to manage workforce access across accounts. It replaces per-account IAM users for human access.

definition: Allows workloads outside AWS (on-premises, other clouds) to obtain temporary AWS credentials using X.509 certificates from a trusted CA.
gotcha: Requires a trust anchor (CA certificate) registered with IAM Roles Anywhere. The workload exchanges its certificate for temporary role credentials.

definition: An organization-level policy that sets the maximum permissions boundary for accounts in AWS Organizations. SCPs don't grant permissions — they limit what IAM policies can grant.
gotcha: SCPs never affect the management account, even when attached to the root OU. They also cannot restrict service-linked roles. Max 5 SCPs per OU/account, 5,120 characters each.

definition: Effective permissions = SCP ∩ IAM policy ∩ Permissions boundary. An action must be allowed by ALL layers. If any layer denies or doesn't allow, the action is denied.
gotcha: A user with AdministratorAccess (Allow *) in a member account can still be blocked by an SCP. The SCP always wins for member accounts.

definition: A KMS key you create, own, and manage. Supports CloudTrail logging, configurable rotation, cross-account sharing, and custom key policies. Costs $1/month + per-use fees.
gotcha: Only customer managed keys allow you to control the rotation schedule and key policy. AWS managed keys rotate automatically every 365 days and you can't change this.

definition: A two-tier encryption pattern: KMS generates a data key → you encrypt data locally with the data key → store the KMS-encrypted copy of the data key alongside the encrypted data.
gotcha: KMS never sees your plaintext data. The 4 KB KMS encrypt limit means you MUST use envelope encryption for anything larger. This is how S3 SSE-KMS, EBS encryption, etc. work internally.

definition: KMS keys replicated across regions sharing the same key material (mrk- prefix). Data encrypted in one region can be decrypted in another without cross-region API calls.
gotcha: Multi-region keys are not global — you must explicitly replicate them to each region you need. They're billed separately in each region.

definition: A stateful virtual firewall at the ENI (instance) level. Supports allow rules only. All rules are evaluated before making a decision. Return traffic is automatically allowed.
gotcha: The default SG allows all inbound from members of the SAME security group and all outbound. A NEW custom SG denies all inbound, allows all outbound. Can reference other SGs as sources.

definition: A stateless firewall at the subnet level. Supports both allow and deny rules. Rules are evaluated in ascending number order — first match wins.
gotcha: Because NACLs are stateless, you must explicitly allow ephemeral ports (1024-65535) outbound for responses to work. The default NACL allows all traffic; custom NACLs deny all by default.

definition: A service for storing, rotating, and managing secrets like database credentials and API keys. Supports automatic rotation via Lambda with native RDS/Redshift/DocumentDB integration.
gotcha: Costs $0.40/secret/month vs Parameter Store Standard which is free. Use Secrets Manager only when you need automatic rotation or cross-region replication. Supports up to 65 KB per secret.

definition: A hierarchical key-value store in AWS Systems Manager. Standard tier is free (up to 10,000 params, 4 KB each). Supports String, StringList, and SecureString (KMS-encrypted) types.
gotcha: No built-in rotation. Advanced tier ($0.05/param/month) raises limits to 100,000 params and 8 KB, but once you upgrade a parameter to Advanced, you cannot downgrade it.

definition: A free VPC endpoint for S3 and DynamoDB only. Adds a route to your route table pointing to the endpoint. No ENI created, no PrivateLink.
gotcha: Gateway endpoints ONLY work from within the VPC — they cannot be accessed from on-premises networks via VPN or Direct Connect, or from peered VPCs. Interface endpoints can.

definition: Creates an ENI with a private IP in your subnet to access AWS services privately. Supports security groups and endpoint policies. Hourly + per-GB charges.
gotcha: Used for most AWS services (KMS, STS, SQS, CloudWatch, etc.) — everything except S3 and DynamoDB (which use Gateway endpoints, though S3 also supports Interface endpoints).

definition: Free, automatic DDoS protection against common Layer 3/4 attacks (SYN floods, UDP reflection) for all AWS customers. No configuration needed.
gotcha: Shield Standard is always on and free — if the exam asks 'at no additional cost' for DDoS protection, this is the answer. It does NOT provide Layer 7 protection or SRT access.

definition: $3,000/month per organization (1-year commitment). Provides L3/4 + L7 DDoS protection, SRT access, DDoS cost protection credits, and advanced metrics.
gotcha: SRT (Shield Response Team) access requires a Business or Enterprise Support plan — just having Shield Advanced is not enough. DDoS cost protection gives service credits, not automatic refunds.

definition: Layer 7 web application firewall. Protects CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito, App Runner, Verified Access, and Amplify. Blocks SQL injection, XSS, and rate-limits requests.
gotcha: WAF does NOT protect EC2 instances directly — only through a supported resource like CloudFront or ALB. Default limit is 1,500 WCU per web ACL.

definition: A managed, highly-available gateway that allows instances in private subnets to access the internet for outbound traffic (updates, API calls) while preventing inbound connections from the internet.
gotcha: NAT Gateways are per-AZ. For HA, deploy one per AZ and route each private subnet to its local NAT Gateway. They charge hourly + per-GB processed. They don't support security groups.

definition: RDS deployment with a synchronous standby replica in a different AZ for high availability. Automatic failover (60-120s for single standby, <35s for DB cluster). The standby is NOT readable in single standby mode.
gotcha: Multi-AZ single standby does NOT serve read traffic — don't confuse it with read replicas. Multi-AZ DB cluster (newer) has 2 readable standbys but only supports MySQL 8.0.28+ and PostgreSQL 13.4+.

definition: An asynchronous copy of an RDS instance that serves read-only traffic. Up to 5 replicas per source (15 for Aurora). Can be cross-region. Can be promoted to a standalone DB (breaks replication).
gotcha: Read replicas use async replication, so they have replication lag (eventual consistency). Multi-AZ standby uses sync replication. If an exam question mentions 'no stale data', read replicas may not be the answer.

term: DynamoDB Partition Key vs Sort Key
definition: Partition key determines which partition stores the item (must distribute evenly). Sort key is optional and orders items within a partition. Together they form the composite primary key.
gotcha: With a composite key (partition + sort), items can share the same partition key but must have unique sort keys. Queries on partition key are fast; queries on sort key alone require a full scan unless you have a GSI.

definition: GSI: different partition/sort key from table, eventually consistent only, 20 per table, add/remove anytime. LSI: same partition key different sort key, supports strongly consistent reads, 5 per table, must create at table creation.
gotcha: LSIs CANNOT be added after table creation. If you realize you need an LSI later, you must recreate the table. LSIs also have a 10 GB limit per partition key value. GSIs are more flexible but only eventually consistent.

definition: On-demand: pay-per-request, instant auto-scaling, no capacity planning. Provisioned: set RCU/WCU, use Auto Scaling, more cost-effective for predictable workloads. Can switch modes once per 24 hours.
gotcha: 1 RCU = 1 strongly consistent read/sec for items up to 4 KB (or 2 eventually consistent reads). 1 WCU = 1 write/sec for items up to 1 KB. Items larger than these sizes consume multiple units.

definition: Standard (frequent), Standard-IA (30-day min, 128KB min), One Zone-IA (1 AZ), Intelligent-Tiering (auto), Glacier Instant (90-day min, ms), Glacier Flexible (90-day min, min-hrs), Glacier Deep Archive (180-day min, 12-48hrs).
gotcha: Early deletion fees apply: if you delete an IA object before 30 days, or a Glacier object before 90/180 days, you're charged for the full minimum duration. Minimum object size charges apply to IA classes (128 KB).

definition: Automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage patterns. No retrieval fees. Charges a small monthly monitoring fee per object. Objects <128 KB stay in Frequent Access tier.
gotcha: Best for unknown or changing access patterns. For KNOWN patterns, a lifecycle policy with specific transitions is more cost-effective (no monitoring fee). Has optional archive tiers you must enable.

definition: CRR (Cross-Region Replication): copies objects to a bucket in a different region — for DR, compliance, or latency. SRR (Same-Region Replication): copies within the same region — for log aggregation or test/prod sync.
gotcha: Both require versioning on source AND destination buckets. Replication is not retroactive — only new objects after enabling are replicated. Delete markers can optionally be replicated.

definition: Standard: unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO: exactly-once processing, strict ordering per message group. Standard FIFO: 300 TPS; High-throughput FIFO: up to 70,000/s.
gotcha: FIFO queue names must end in .fifo. Standard queues may deliver duplicates, so your consumer must be idempotent. FIFO queues have a 5-minute deduplication window.

definition: An SNS topic publishes a message to multiple SQS queue subscribers. Each queue gets its own copy of the message for independent processing.
gotcha: Don't confuse with a single SQS queue with multiple consumers — that's competing consumers where each message goes to ONE consumer. Fan-out ensures ALL subscribers get every message.

definition: Serverless event bus for event-driven architectures. Routes events from AWS services, custom apps, and SaaS partners to targets using content-based filtering rules. Supports scheduling, archive, and replay.
gotcha: EventBridge replaces CloudWatch Events (same underlying service). Use EventBridge over SNS when you need content-based filtering, schema discovery, event archive/replay, or SaaS partner integration.

definition: ALB: Layer 7, HTTP/HTTPS routing (path, host, header), Lambda targets, auth (OIDC/Cognito). NLB: Layer 4, TCP/UDP/TLS, static IPs, ultra-high performance, PrivateLink support.
gotcha: ALB does NOT support static/Elastic IPs. If an exam question mentions 'static IP' or 'whitelisting by IP', the answer is NLB. If it mentions 'path-based routing' or 'authentication', the answer is ALB.

definition: Target Tracking (maintain metric at target value, e.g., 70% CPU). Step Scaling (scale by amount based on alarm thresholds). Scheduled (scale at specific times). Predictive (ML-based forecast).
gotcha: Target tracking is simplest and recommended for most cases. You cannot use target tracking with the same metric as step scaling. Cooldown periods prevent rapid scale-in/out oscillation.

definition: Cheapest DR strategy. Store backups in another region. Restore from backups when disaster occurs. Highest RTO (hours) and RPO (hours to last backup).
gotcha: This is the only DR strategy with zero running costs in the DR region (just storage). But RTO can be many hours depending on data volume and infrastructure provisioning time.

definition: Core infrastructure (database, replication) running in DR region, but application servers are off. Scale up on failover. RTO: tens of minutes. Lower cost than Warm Standby.
gotcha: The 'light' is the database — it's the minimal critical component kept running. Application and web tiers must be provisioned during failover, which takes time. Exam may contrast this with Warm Standby.

definition: A scaled-down but fully functional copy of the production environment running in the DR region. Scale up to production size on failover. RTO: minutes.
gotcha: The key difference from Pilot Light: Warm Standby has ALL tiers running (just smaller), while Pilot Light only has the data tier running. Warm Standby costs more but recovers faster.

definition: Full production environments in multiple regions, both actively serving traffic. Data is synchronously or near-synchronously replicated. Near-zero RPO and RTO. Most expensive.
gotcha: This is the only strategy that provides near-zero RPO/RTO. If the exam mentions 'near-zero downtime' or 'no data loss', this is likely the answer. Route 53 handles traffic distribution.

definition: RPO (Recovery Point Objective): maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (how far back can you lose?). RTO (Recovery Time Objective): maximum acceptable downtime (how fast must you recover?).
gotcha: RPO is about DATA LOSS, RTO is about DOWNTIME. A lower RPO requires more frequent backups or replication. A lower RTO requires more standby infrastructure (and more cost).

definition: Identity-based policies attach to users/groups/roles and say what that identity can do. Resource-based policies attach to resources (S3 buckets, SQS queues) and specify which principals can access them. Within the same account, either alone is sufficient. Cross-account requires both.
gotcha: Resource-based policies have a Principal field; identity-based policies do not. For cross-account access, both the identity's account AND the resource's account must grant permission.

definition: A global service that issues temporary security credentials (access key, secret key, and session token) when a principal assumes a role. STS itself does not authorize actions — the role's permission policy does.
gotcha: STS credentials expire automatically (15 min to 12 hours). Role chaining via STS caps sessions at 1 hour regardless of the role's max session setting.

definition: The STS API call used to obtain temporary credentials for an IAM role. Requires the caller to be listed in the role's trust policy. Returns an access key, secret key, and session token.
gotcha: AssumeRole requires BOTH the trust policy on the role to allow the caller AND the caller's own IAM policy to permit sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN (for cross-account). Missing either side = Access Denied.

definition: A resource-based policy on an IAM role that defines which principals (users, roles, accounts, or services) can call sts:AssumeRole to assume the role. It is the 'door lock' — who can get in.
gotcha: The trust policy controls WHO can assume the role. The permission policy controls WHAT the role can do. Exam questions often test whether you know which policy to fix when access fails.

definition: A Deny statement in any applicable policy. Explicit Deny ALWAYS overrides any Allow statement anywhere. Evaluation order: Explicit Deny > Allow > Implicit Deny (default no-permission state).
gotcha: If any policy (SCP, permissions boundary, identity policy, resource policy) has an explicit Deny for an action, that action is denied — period. No amount of Allow statements can override it.

definition: Grant only the minimum permissions required for a task. Start with zero permissions and add only what is needed. Use IAM Access Analyzer and last-accessed data to identify and remove unused permissions.
gotcha: The exam loves answers that follow least privilege. If one answer uses a broad wildcard (*) policy and another scopes to specific actions/resources, the scoped answer is usually correct.

definition: An advanced IAM feature that sets the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can have. Does not grant permissions — only limits what identity-based policies can grant. Think of it as a ceiling on permissions.
gotcha: Effective permissions = intersection of identity policy AND permissions boundary. If the boundary allows s3:* but the identity policy only allows s3:GetObject, the user can only GetObject. Commonly tested in delegated-admin scenarios.

definition: Provides temporary AWS credentials to mobile/web app users who sign in via social providers (Google, Facebook, Apple), SAML, or OpenID Connect. Uses web identity federation to exchange tokens for STS credentials scoped by an IAM role.
gotcha: Cognito is for CUSTOMER-FACING app users. IAM Identity Center is for WORKFORCE (employee) users. If the exam mentions mobile apps + social login, Cognito is the answer.

definition: A free service that lets you group multiple AWS accounts under a single management structure. Provides consolidated billing, organizational units (OUs), and policy-based governance via SCPs. One management account controls the organization.
gotcha: Organizations is required for SCPs. Without enabling 'all features' mode, only consolidated billing is available — SCPs are not. You can invite existing accounts or create new ones from the management account.

definition: The single account that created the AWS Organization. It pays the consolidated bill, can create/invite member accounts, and manages SCPs. It is exempt from SCP restrictions.
gotcha: SCPs NEVER restrict the management account — not even SCPs attached to the root OU. Best practice: use it only for billing and org management, never for workloads, because it operates without SCP guardrails.

definition: Any AWS account in an organization that is not the management account. Member accounts are subject to SCPs. They can be created by the organization or invited into it.
gotcha: SCPs apply to ALL principals in member accounts, including the root user. This is unlike normal IAM where the root user cannot be restricted by IAM policies. The member account root user IS restricted by SCPs.

definition: A container within AWS Organizations that groups accounts. OUs can be nested. SCPs attached to an OU are inherited by all accounts and child OUs beneath it. Common OUs: Production, Development, Security, Shared Services.
gotcha: Moving an account between OUs instantly changes which SCPs apply to it. If users in an account suddenly lose access, check whether the account was recently moved to an OU with more restrictive SCPs.

definition: SCPs flow down the organization hierarchy: root → OU → child OU → account. The effective SCP for any account is the intersection of all SCPs from the root to that account. A child can never have more permissions than its parent allows.
gotcha: An explicit Deny at any level cannot be overridden by an Allow at a lower level. A more permissive SCP on a child OU does NOT expand beyond the parent's ceiling. Permissions only narrow as you descend.

definition: Deny-list (default): keep FullAWSAccess SCP and add explicit Deny for blocked actions. Allow-list: remove FullAWSAccess and explicitly Allow only permitted services — everything else is implicitly denied.
gotcha: If you remove FullAWSAccess without a replacement Allow SCP, ALL actions are denied for member accounts. A deny-list SCP alone (without FullAWSAccess) does not allow anything — the broad Allow comes from FullAWSAccess, not from the absence of Deny.

definition: All member accounts' charges roll into one bill paid by the management account. Enables volume pricing discounts (S3, data transfer) and Reserved Instance sharing across the organization.
gotcha: Consolidated billing is a COST feature, not a SECURITY feature. It does not enforce permissions, restrict actions, or provide guardrails. If the exam asks about 'centralized security enforcement,' the answer is SCPs, not consolidated billing.

definition: A KMS key created and managed by AWS in your account for a specific service (alias: aws/<service>). You can view it and see CloudTrail logs, but you cannot change its policy, rotation, or share it cross-account.
gotcha: AWS managed keys CANNOT be shared cross-account because you cannot modify the key policy. For cross-account encrypted resource sharing (snapshots, S3 objects), you MUST use a customer managed key.

definition: A KMS key owned and managed entirely by AWS in a service account. Invisible to you — no CloudTrail logging, no key policy control. Used for default encryption in many services. Completely free.
gotcha: You cannot view, manage, audit, or rotate AWS owned keys. If the exam asks about auditing key usage or controlling encryption key access, AWS owned keys are not the answer.

term: Encryption at Rest vs In Transit
definition: At rest: protects data stored on disk/database (KMS, SSE). In transit: protects data moving over networks (TLS/HTTPS, VPN). They are independent — enabling one does NOT enable the other.
gotcha: A common exam trap: 'data is encrypted with KMS' only means at rest. Data still travels in plaintext unless TLS/SSL is separately configured. The exam tests whether you know these are separate concerns.

definition: SSE-S3: S3 manages keys, no visibility/control, free. SSE-KMS: KMS manages keys, CloudTrail audit, key policy access control, per-request cost. SSE-C: you provide the key with every request, AWS never stores it, HTTPS required.
gotcha: SSE-S3 is the default since Jan 2023. SSE-KMS adds audit + access control but costs more and is subject to KMS request quotas. SSE-C requires you to manage and provide the key — lose the key, lose the data.

definition: Symmetric (default): single 256-bit AES-GCM key for encrypt and decrypt. Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA or ECC) for encryption outside AWS or digital signing. AWS service integrations require symmetric keys.
gotcha: You CANNOT use an asymmetric KMS key with S3 SSE-KMS, EBS encryption, RDS encryption, etc. — they all require symmetric keys. Asymmetric keys are for external encryption or digital signing where the caller can't call KMS.

definition: A resource-based policy attached directly to a KMS key. It is the PRIMARY access control for the key. Without key policy permission, even the account root user cannot use the key (unlike most AWS resources).
gotcha: By default, the key policy grants the root account full access and enables IAM policies to work. If someone removes this default statement, IAM policies alone cannot grant KMS access — the key becomes manageable only through the key policy.

definition: Automatic rotation creates new cryptographic material while keeping the same key ID/ARN. Old material is preserved for decrypting old data. Customer managed keys: optional, configurable interval. AWS managed keys: automatic yearly.
gotcha: Rotation does NOT re-encrypt existing data. Old data still uses old key material (preserved by KMS). If compliance requires current material on all data, you must re-encrypt existing data manually.

definition: Permanently destroys a KMS key and all its cryptographic material. Irreversible. AWS enforces a 7-30 day waiting period before deletion. During the wait, you can cancel. After deletion, all data encrypted under the key is permanently unrecoverable.
gotcha: There is NO way to recover a deleted KMS key or the data it protected. This is the most dangerous KMS operation. Disable the key first (reversible) before considering deletion.

definition: KMS: fully managed, multi-tenant HSMs, deep AWS service integration, $1/key/month. CloudHSM: you manage HSM clusters, single-tenant, FIPS 140-2 Level 3, custom integration via PKCS#11/JCE/CNG, ~$1.50/hr per HSM.
gotcha: CloudHSM is for regulatory requirements demanding single-tenant hardware and exclusive key control. If the exam says 'dedicated hardware' or 'PKCS#11', the answer is CloudHSM. For everything else, KMS.

definition: A symmetric key generated by KMS (via GenerateDataKey) used to encrypt actual data locally. KMS returns both a plaintext copy and a KMS-encrypted copy. You encrypt data with the plaintext key, then discard it and store only the encrypted copy.
gotcha: The data key encrypts the data. The KMS key encrypts the data key. KMS never sees your data — only the small data key. This two-tier pattern is called envelope encryption and is how S3 SSE-KMS, EBS, and RDS encryption work internally.
